sections.h2: What are the options for selling a house in Burbank?
sections.html:
A Burbank homeowner can list on the open market, sell privately, or accept a direct cash purchase. The city is small and almost entirely residential, and nearly 81 percent of its housing units are owner-occupied, so most sales are between one household and the next.

  • Open-market listing: the usual route when the house shows well and you can wait through a buyer's loan approval.
  • Private sale: skips the agent's fee, but you manage the contract, the deed and the city transfer paperwork.
  • Cash purchase: fits inherited houses, houses with deferred repairs, or a seller who needs a fixed closing day.

Every route runs through the Burbank City Clerk for the city's real estate transfer tax, and through the Cook County Clerk's Recordings Division for the deed. Ask your title company which of those errands it will run for you and which fall to you as the seller.

sections.h2: What is Burbank, Illinois, and how was it built?
sections.html:
Burbank is a Cook County city of 4.17 square miles in Stickney Township, southwest of Chicago, with ZIP code 60459. Its land stayed mostly farmland for a century, with 1920s subdivision plans stalling on drainage problems, thin water and sewer service and then the Great Depression.

Real building began in the 1950s. The area had about 20,720 residents by 1960, nearly triple the count of a decade earlier, and it incorporated as a city on April 4, 1970, partly to resist annexation by Chicago. The name comes from Luther Burbank Elementary School, which had served the area since the 1930s. Population peaked at 29,448 in 1976 and stood at 29,439 in the 2020 census.

Because most of the area was built out after 1950, a buyer's inspector will be looking at houses that are 70 years old or close to it, and the age of roofs, furnaces and plumbing is the first thing that comes up.

sections.h2: What do Census numbers show for Burbank homes?
sections.html:
The Census Bureau reports a median owner-occupied value of $275,700 in Burbank, with 80.9 percent of homes occupied by their owners and 9,539 households. Its July 1, 2025 estimate of 28,578 residents is 3.0 percent below the 2020 base.

sections.h2: Does Burbank charge a real estate transfer tax?
sections.html:
Yes. The City Clerk's page lists Burbank real estate transfer tax forms, updated in 2024, and the clerk's office at 6530 W 79th Street handles them. Call 708-599-5500 before closing to confirm the amount, the forms and any other village requirement.

The clerk's hours are Monday, Wednesday, Thursday and Friday from 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m., Tuesday from 8:30 a.m. to 6 p.m., and closed on weekends. The page also lists 2026 office closures, including Veterans Day and the day after Thanksgiving, so plan a stamp pickup around them. Ask the clerk for the current rate, who pays it and the list of exempt transfers.

Illinois sets its own base tax at 50 cents per $500 of value, collected by the county, and counties may add 25 cents per $500 under the Department of Revenue's description.

sections.h2: How does the Burbank Building Department affect a sale?
sections.html:
The Building Department at City Hall, reached at 708-599-5500 option 2, decides whether work needs a permit, and a buyer will ask whether past work was permitted. The city says permits are needed for roof replacement, fences, siding, driveways, porches, furnaces, air conditioning, plumbing, electrical work and any remodeling.

  • The city says all contractors must be licensed to do any type of work in Burbank.
  • Replacing a gas water heater calls for a no-charge inspection of venting, the safety valve and the connection.
  • Garage sales are limited to two a year, not allowed on Sundays, and need a permit.

Before listing, gather permit paperwork for any roof, furnace or addition. If work was done without one, ask the department what is needed to regularize it, since an unpermitted change can slow a conventional sale and is a common reason owners pick a buyer who takes the house as it stands.

sections.h2: How is Burbank governed and how does that matter to sellers?
sections.html:
Burbank uses an aldermanic city form of government, with a mayor, city clerk, treasurer and seven aldermen, all elected to four-year terms. The City Council meets on the second and fourth Tuesday of each month at 6:00 p.m. in the Council Chambers on the second floor of City Hall.

Those meetings are open to the public and take comments before adjournment, which is where a resident with a code or zoning question can be heard. The Building Commissioner's office also handles property maintenance, code enforcement and zoning reviews, so a house with an open violation should be dealt with before it goes under contract.

sections.h2: What paperwork should a Burbank seller gather before closing?
sections.html:
A Burbank sale needs a short stack of documents, and having them ready keeps a closing on schedule. The title company or attorney handles most of it, but the seller supplies the permit history and the identity of the owners of record.

  • The deed, so the recording office and the city clerk can match the owners.
  • The Illinois PTAX-203 transfer declaration, completed by buyer and seller and filed in the county where the property sits.
  • The city's real estate transfer tax form from the City Clerk's page.
  • Permit records for roof, furnace, electrical or plumbing work.
  • Your most recent Cook County property tax bill.

The Cook County Assessor explains that exemptions appear as deductions on the second installment bill. If you are unsure whether a homeowner or senior exemption is in place, ask the Cook County Treasurer or Assessor before closing, since it affects the tax proration on the settlement statement. The Recordings Division's site also lists recording fees, which are set by state and county ordinances, and a Recordings Legal Help Desk where a volunteer attorney can answer recording questions.

sections.h2: How does Burbank's location help with showing a house?
sections.html:
Burbank is served by Pace bus routes that connect it with the southwest side of Chicago and the south suburbs, and the Census Bureau puts the mean commute at 31.3 minutes.

The city is also diverse: Census Bureau figures show 51.1 percent of residents identify as Hispanic or Latino and 60.9 percent of residents age 5 and older speak a language other than English at home. Offering Spanish-language materials and a translator at showings reaches buyers a plain English flyer would miss.

faqs.q: Where do I get Burbank transfer tax forms?
faqs.a: From the City Clerk's page on burbankil.gov, which posts the transfer tax forms as a two-page PDF updated in 2024, or at the clerk's office at 6530 W 79th Street. Call 708-599-5500 to confirm what is needed.

faqs.q: What are the clerk's office hours in Burbank?
faqs.a: Monday, Wednesday, Thursday and Friday are 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m., and Tuesday is 8:30 a.m. to 6 p.m. The office is closed Saturday and Sunday and on listed holidays.

faqs.q: Which county records a Burbank deed?
faqs.a: Cook County. The Cook County Clerk's Recordings Division keeps the land records, with office hours of 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. and the last customer accepted at 4:45 p.m.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for a new roof in Burbank?
faqs.a: Yes. The Building Department lists roof replacement among the work that needs a permit. Call 708-599-5500, option 2, to confirm the steps for your house.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Burbank house that has repair problems?
faqs.a: Yes. Many buyers, including cash buyers, purchase houses as they stand. Gather permit records, ask the Building Department about open items, and compare offers on the net amount after repairs.
